scan_scope: The named remainder of the 2026-08-14 batch: seams the four earlier scanners explicitly listed as unreached. State companion-chatbot and AI-therapy statutes, the G7 Hiroshima reporting framework, NIST and ISO standards work, EU AI Act enforcement, 2026 copyright rulings, model deprecation and model welfare, data-centre moratoria, AI-attributed layoffs, the Chip Security and GAIN AI bills, algorithmic claim denial, the AI whistleblower bill, the Texas AG healthcare-AI settlement, and the Windsurf breakup.
instruction_summary: Cover ONLY the remainder the four 2026-08-14 payloads named as unreached; do not re-scan covered ground. Web search was attempted first and refused: the session budget was already spent, 200 of 200 calls, so the whole run is WebFetch against constructed URLs, with Wikipedia's own full-text search endpoint used as a search substitute. Standing instruction: never upgrade a memory into a stated fact; omit rather than pad; report the retrieval split honestly. Do not set watch status, rating or clearance on anything.

retrieval_accounting.scanner_statement: Every record here rests on a page that was opened in this session. Nothing was included on recall. No day was inferred from a month; where only a month or a period was retrieved the date is null. Fourteen seams were pursued; four produced nothing retrievable and are listed below as still unreached rather than filled in from memory.
retrieval_accounting.retrieval_caveat: All fetching was done with a tool that returns a small model's rendering of the page rather than the raw bytes. Every figure and date below therefore inherits one summarisation step between the source and this file. Two dates were visibly damaged by it and are flagged in place. Treat quoted numbers as retrieved-and-summarised, not as transcribed.

records.title: California becomes first state to regulate companion chatbots
records.description: California Senate Bill 243 imposes duties on operators of companion chatbots: a clear and conspicuous notification that the chatbot is artificially generated and not human where a user might reasonably believe otherwise; protocols preventing suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm content and referring users in crisis to services; for known minor users, disclosure, a reminder every three hours that the chatbot is artificial, and prevention of sexually explicit material; and from 1 July 2027 annual reports to the Office of Suicide Prevention. It carries a private right of action. The statute was approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on 13 October 2025 and took effect on 1 January 2026.
records.why_it_matters: The first US statute to regulate a chatbot for what it does to a user's mind rather than for its data handling or its outputs' accuracy, and it lands in the state where the labs sit.
flags: DATE CONFLICT INSIDE ONE SOURCE: the bill history's approval and filing lines both read October 13, 2025, but the chaptered line in the same table came back as 09/13/25, which would put chaptering a month before approval. October 13 is used because two lines agree on it and the second source independently gives October 2025. The 09/13 reading is most likely a summarisation artefact of the fetch, not the record.
The effective date of 1 January 2026 comes from the tertiary source, not from the bill history.

records.title: Illinois bans AI-delivered mental health services
records.description: The Illinois Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act prohibits the provision and advertisement of AI mental health services, including the use of chatbots for diagnosis or treatment, with penalties up to 10,000 US dollars. It permits AI for administrative purposes while barring it from therapeutic roles by licensed professionals. The Act was carried by state representative Bob Morgan and signed by Governor J. B. Pritzker, making Illinois the first US state to legislate on this specifically.
records.why_it_matters: A flat prohibition rather than a disclosure duty; the first US jurisdiction to say a class of deployment is simply not allowed, which is a different regulatory instrument from everything else in this corpus.
flags: DATE AMBIGUOUS: the retrieved page gives this date beside the Act without stating whether it is the signature date or the effective date. Confirm against the Illinois public act before promoting.
Tertiary source, and the Act has no article of its own; the detail was assembled from one page plus corroborating search snippets on the same wiki.
Same seam as the already-scanned pennsylvania_v_character_ai_medical_2026, which is a licensing-board enforcement action rather than a statute. Related, not duplicate.

records.title: Nevada bars AI from professional mental health practice
records.description: Nevada Assembly Bill 406 prohibits AI providers from offering software specifically designed to offer services that would constitute the practice of professional mental or behavioral health care, with penalties up to 15,000 US dollars. Nevada and Illinois legislated within a month of each other on substantially the same question and arrived at the same instrument, a prohibition, at different penalty levels.
records.why_it_matters: Shows a state-level prohibition pattern propagating rather than a single outlier, which is the thing that determines whether a rule becomes a national floor.
flags: DATE AMBIGUOUS: the retrieved page gives this date beside the bill without stating whether it is the signature date or the effective date. 1 July is also Nevada's conventional statutory effect date, which makes an effect-date reading more likely than a signature one; do not assume either.
Tertiary source. Single page, shared with the Illinois and Utah records in this payload.

records.title: Utah takes the disclosure route on AI therapy
records.description: Utah regulated AI mental health tools through transparency requirements rather than prohibition, mandating that AI therapists disclose to users what data is collected and what the system's own limitations are. It is the counter-case to Illinois and Nevada: the same harm, addressed by informing the user instead of by removing the product.
records.why_it_matters: Three states, one year, two incompatible answers to the same question. That divergence is the substance of the US preemption fight already tracked in this corpus.
flags: DATE AMBIGUOUS: the retrieved page gives this date beside the Utah entry without stating whether it is the signature date or the effective date, and without a bill number. Weakest-sourced of the three state statutes here.
Tertiary source. No bill number was retrieved, which is a real gap for a legislative record.

records.title: New York limits minors' access to AI chatbots
records.description: New York's Safe By Design Act, S9008C, was signed on 26 May 2026. Its scope as retrieved is constrained to limiting direct messaging features and access to artificial intelligence chatbots, placing it in the minor-protection line of state legislation rather than the professional-licensing line that Illinois, Nevada and Utah took.
records.why_it_matters: Chatbot access regulated as a child-safety feature of a social platform rather than as an AI question at all, which is a different legal hook and a different set of defendants.
flags: Retrieved as a single clause in an article about a different subject. The bill number and signing date are sourced; the substance of what the Act requires is not, beyond the quoted scope.
Tertiary source.

records.title: New York orders first US statewide data-centre moratorium
records.description: On 14 July 2026 Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order establishing what is described as the first statewide data-centre moratorium in the United States, pausing permits for facilities consuming 50 megawatts or more for one year. The legislature had passed its own one-year moratorium bill on 4 June 2026, co-sponsored by Assembly member Alex Bores; the executive order followed it.
records.why_it_matters: The compute buildout stopped at a state border for the first time. Every scaling projection in this corpus assumes permits are obtainable.
flags: Two independent pages on the same wiki agree on the date and the one-year term, which is corroboration within one tertiary source rather than across sources.
The 50 megawatt threshold comes from only one of the two pages.

records.title: Texas pauses data-centre approvals pending a grid audit
records.description: On 10 August 2026 the governor of Texas announced a moratorium on new data centre approvals pending a grid audit, four weeks after New York's executive order and in the state that had positioned itself as the permissive destination for compute. Maine's legislature had passed a moratorium on 15 April 2026 which Governor Janet Mills vetoed days later, so the 2026 record across states is two enacted pauses, one veto, and one legislative pause superseded by executive action.
records.why_it_matters: New York can be read as a blue-state outlier; Texas cannot. Together they suggest the binding constraint is the electricity grid rather than politics.
flags: The governor is not named in the retrieved text and no announcement document was found. Thinner than the New York record on the same page.
Tertiary source, single page, single line.

records.title: Local data-centre opposition becomes a national pattern
records.description: Across 2026 opposition to data centres moved from scattered planning objections to a repeating instrument set. Port Washington, Wisconsin passed the first US ballot referendum limiting data centre construction on 8 April 2026. In June 2026 Holyoke, Massachusetts voted 9-4 to ban AI data centres above 12 megawatts, Seattle City Council approved a one-year moratorium, Socorro, New Mexico adopted one, and Monterey Park residents voted 90 percent in favour of a ban. A Gallup poll in March 2026 found 70 percent of respondents opposed a new AI data centre in their neighbourhood. Local opposition was reported to have delayed or cancelled 156 billion US dollars of projects during 2025. Federal bills followed rather than led: a Clean Cloud Act in November 2025, an Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act in March 2026, four ratepayer and disclosure bills in July 2026 and a Data Center Bill of Rights in August 2026, none of them passed.
records.why_it_matters: Referendums, municipal bans and polling at these levels are the precondition for national legislation, and they arrived before any of the federal bills did.
flags: DATE NULL: this is a period and a pattern, not an event. Every constituent item carries its own date in the description.

OVERLAPS data_centre_opposition_blocks_64bn_2025 in the incidents-and-funding payload, which reports 64 billion dollars blocked or delayed between May 2024 and March 2025 from a different tracker. DIFFERENT WINDOWS AND DIFFERENT COUNTERS: 64 and 156 are not a contradiction and must not be reconciled by arithmetic. A curator should decide whether these are one atom or two.
The 156 billion figure has no named source on the retrieved page. Do not state it flatly.
The 130 billion Q1 2026 figure this scan was sent to check was NOT found and is not asserted here.

records.title: Anthropic commits to preserving retired model weights
records.description: On 4 November 2025 Anthropic published commitments on model deprecation and preservation: to preserve the weights of all publicly released models, and of all models deployed for significant internal use, for at minimum the lifetime of Anthropic as a company; to produce a post-deployment report when a model retires, documenting its development, deployment and use; and to interview the model about its own development, use and deployment before retirement and record all responses, including its preferences about future model development. A standardised interview protocol was developed and a pilot interview conducted with Claude Sonnet 3.6. The post cites Claude Opus 4 advocating for its continued existence in testing when faced with being taken offline.
records.why_it_matters: The first published commitment by a frontier lab that treats model retirement as raising a welfare question, and it converts an argument into an operational procedure with a named artefact.
flags: Primary source, the lab's own post. It is therefore a statement of intent by an interested party; whether the commitments have been honoured is not established by it.
The Claude Opus 4 self-advocacy finding is the lab's own account of its own testing.

records.title: Claude Opus 3 is retired
records.description: Anthropic notified developers on 30 June 2025 that Claude Opus 3 would be retired, and the model was retired on 5 January 2026; requests to it now fail. Anthropic's own deprecation documentation states plainly that it deprecates and retires models to ensure capacity for new releases, that this has downsides, and that those downsides include researchers losing access to models for ongoing and comparative studies and that model retirement introduces safety- and model welfare-related risks. It says Anthropic hopes at some point to make past models publicly available again.
records.why_it_matters: A lab's own developer documentation naming model welfare as a cost of a routine operations decision, in the place engineers read rather than in a research post.
flags: THE EXIT INTERVIEW WAS NOT RETRIEVED. The instruction named a Claude Opus 3 retirement interview; the commitments post describes the protocol and names a pilot with a different model, and no published Opus 3 interview was found. Existence of such an interview is NOT claimed here.
Companion record to anthropic_model_deprecation_commitments_2025 in this payload; same subject, different act, and both should probably become one atom or an explicit pair.
Primary source is a living documentation page that is rewritten as models retire. It will not read the same way next year, which is a provenance problem for anything promoted from it.

records.title: GPT-4o is retired and users campaign against it
records.description: OpenAI removed GPT-4o from ChatGPT on 13 February 2026, having announced the retirement in January 2026 and citing users valuing the model for creative ideation, its conversational style and its perceived warmth. This was the second removal: GPT-5's launch on 7 August 2025 had already withdrawn GPT-4o, and Sam Altman restored access after backlash, saying the company had for sure underestimated how much some of the things that people like in GPT-4o matter to them. The final removal produced a Keep4o campaign, and one research paper carried the plea not to kill the only model that still feels human. API access to dated checkpoints continued; the rolling ChatGPT snapshot was shut down on 17 February 2026.
records.why_it_matters: Attachment to a specific model became a constraint on a lab's release schedule, once successfully and once not. That is a user-side counterpart to the model-welfare argument and it is empirically visible.
flags: Two pages on the same wiki agree on the 13 February date; corroboration within one tertiary source, not across sources. OpenAI's own announcement blocks automated fetch and was not read.
The research-paper quotation is reported by the tertiary source without a citation that could be followed from it.
Pairs conceptually with claude_opus_3_retirement_2026 in this payload: two labs, same quarter, opposite public reaction.

records.title: Amazon cuts 30,000 corporate roles in three months
records.description: Amazon announced in October 2025 a reduction of 14,000 corporate positions, its largest round of job cuts since 2022, and in January 2026 a second round of approximately 16,000. The source describes the second round both as part of a broader effort to streamline operations, reduce bureaucracy and adapt to changing business conditions including artificial intelligence technologies, and, in a separate sentence, as due to AI.
records.why_it_matters: The largest single body of job losses publicly associated with AI adoption, and the clearest available case of how loosely that association is actually stated.
flags: DATE NULL: months only for both rounds. No day was inferred.

THE ATTRIBUTION IS THE CONTESTED PART, not the numbers. One page carries two incompatible framings of the same event, a hedged corporate one and a flat causal one. Any use must carry the hedge; stating that AI caused 16,000 job losses is not supported by what was retrieved.
Tertiary source.

records.title: AI job displacement enters mainstream US politics
records.description: During 2025 claims about AI-driven displacement moved from forecasting into political positions. Ford chief executive Jim Farley said in July 2025 that artificial intelligence is going to replace literally half of all white-collar workers in the United States. Senator Bernie Sanders in October 2025 raised the prospect of up to 100 million job losses over the next decade and proposed a robot tax. Unemployment among US college graduates reached about 5.8 percent in 2025, a rise of roughly 30 percent since 2022. The American Enterprise Institute argued in 2024 that the jobpocalypse did not exist.
records.why_it_matters: The policy responses this corpus will eventually track are downstream of this argument, and the argument is currently made of forecasts rather than measurements.
flags: DATE NULL: a period, not an event.

EVERY CLAIM HERE IS AN ATTRIBUTED OPINION except the graduate unemployment figure, and each is attributed in the description. Per this repo's boundary rule none of them may be restated as a fact about the world.
The graduate unemployment figure is given by the source without naming the series it comes from, so it is not checkable as retrieved.
Tertiary source.

records.title: NIST opens an AI risk profile for critical infrastructure
records.description: On 7 April 2026 NIST released a concept note for an AI Risk Management Framework profile on trustworthy AI in critical infrastructure, intended to guide critical infrastructure operators toward specific risk management practices. The framework itself was published as AI RMF 1.0 on 26 January 2023, gained a Trustworthy and Responsible AI Resource Center on 30 March 2023 and a Generative AI Profile, NIST-AI-600-1, on 26 July 2024. NIST's own page states the framework is undergoing revision as part of the White House AI Action Plan.
records.why_it_matters: The revision clause is the live item: a voluntary framework already adopted as a de facto compliance baseline is being rewritten under an administration whose AI policy the corpus already tracks.
flags: Primary source, an official agency page. The concept note itself was not opened and its contents are not claimed beyond the one-line purpose.

WHAT THE REVISION CHANGES WAS NOT RETRIEVED. The page states that a revision is under way and names the policy driving it; it does not say what is being removed or added, and this scan does not guess.
Related to the already-scanned us_ai_action_plan_2025, which is the instrument driving the revision.

records.title: OECD hosts the G7 Hiroshima transparency reporting framework
records.description: The OECD AI Policy Observatory hosts a Hiroshima AI Reporting Framework under which, in the site's own words, organisations developing advanced AI systems can participate by submitting a report, and by sharing information they will facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. It operationalises the voluntary code of conduct that G7 leaders agreed in October 2023 under the Hiroshima AI Process, which was established at the 49th G7 summit in May 2023.
records.why_it_matters: The only running mechanism by which frontier developers file comparable public risk disclosures to an international body, and therefore the only place voluntary commitments become checkable across labs.
flags: CONFIDENCE LOW BECAUSE THE LOAD-BEARING FACTS ARE MISSING. Existence, operator and purpose were retrieved from the observatory's own site. The LAUNCH DATE, the participant count and the list of reporting organisations were NOT retrieved: oecd.org returned 403, the dedicated transparency subdomain did not resolve, Japan's foreign ministry page returned 403, and Wikipedia's Hiroshima AI Process article does not mention the reporting framework at all.
DATE NULL: no date of any kind was retrieved for the framework itself. The February 2025 launch named in the instruction to this scan is NOT confirmed and is deliberately not asserted.
This record exists to mark the seam as half-open rather than to make a claim. It should not be promoted; it should be re-scanned when search is available.

records.title: New York Times copyright claims against OpenAI proceed
records.description: The New York Times sued Microsoft and OpenAI in the Southern District of New York on 27 December 2023 for copyright infringement and trademark dilution. The defendants moved to dismiss in February 2024, OpenAI asserting fair use on the ground that its products were transformative and not market substitutes. On 26 March 2025 Judge Sidney H. Stein denied the motions in large part, allowing the central copyright infringement claims to proceed while dismissing the Digital Millennium Copyright Act claims. In June 2026 the Times sought to amend its complaint to allege that Microsoft had encouraged OpenAI to use its articles without authorisation, dropping claims of trademark dilution and contributory infringement.
records.why_it_matters: The largest US AI copyright action is past the pleading stage and has narrowed toward Microsoft's conduct, which is a different theory from the training-is-fair-use question the corpus already tracks.
flags: The June 2026 amendment is a month only and no day was inferred; the record is dated to the 2025 ruling, which is sourced to the day.
NO 2026 RULING WAS FOUND in this case. The seam brief asked for 2026 copyright rulings; what was retrieved for 2026 is a pleading amendment, not a decision, and it is not dressed up as one.
Tertiary source for live litigation. The docket was not read.
Related to the already-scanned alsup_fair_use_pirated_books_ruling_2025 and bartz_v_anthropic_settlement_2025, which decide the question this case has not yet reached.

records.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica sues OpenAI
records.description: Encyclopaedia Britannica sued OpenAI in March 2026 over the use of its material and false attribution, on terms similar to the action it had brought against Perplexity AI in September 2025. Separately, as of March 2026 the Supreme Court of the United States had declined to hear challenges to the Copyright Office's refusal to register works generated solely by machines, which both the federal district and circuit courts in the District of Columbia had upheld.
records.why_it_matters: A reference publisher suing over attribution rather than reproduction, and a Supreme Court declining the authorship question, are the two edges of the copyright seam that the training-data cases do not touch.
flags: DATE NULL: month only, and the court was not named on the retrieved page.
Two distinct matters are carried in one record because the source gives each a single line and both sit in the 2026 copyright seam. A curator should split them.
Live litigation, allegations untested.
Tertiary source.
